title: I Already Do That!
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses the common response to feedback, 'I already do that,' which usually reflects a real gap between what team members believe they do and what others see. It argues that leaders who try to prove the reality with past evidence end up in a debate they cannot win. The recommended move is to ask for recent, specific examples instead of arguing. Team members who truly do the behavior can supply examples quickly, while most will fail to, and that gap becomes the opening for a teaching conversation rather than an 'I told you so.' The piece ends by presenting examples as a lens on true actions and beliefs.
points: The reply 'I already do that' more often reflects unawareness than resistance, so feedback stalls unless it is addressed.
Leaders who try to prove the team member wrong typically start a debate they cannot win in the sense that matters, getting the feedback acted on.
Asking for recent, specific examples lets people either prove their point or discover the omission themselves.
A missing example becomes a collaborative coaching moment rather than a chance to say 'I told you so'.
Examples serve as evidence of understanding, so the question 'Can you give me an example of that?' is a diagnostic tool.
quotes: It’s somewhat surprising to many leaders how often team members who receive actionable feedback and recommendations for improvement respond with, “I already do that!

This answer sometimes reflects a passive resistance to the advice; however, more often than not, the team member truly believes they are already performing the suggested action. They often lack an awareness that what they think they are doing is not what others believe and see. If left unaddressed, this disconnect means little action or improvement will likely be made.

This desperate need to confront the team member and show them their error normally results in a debate the leader does not win, at least not if winning means getting the team member to act on the feedback.
A better strategy to prove the point is simply to ask for examples. Ask how the team member has already incorporated the suggested actions. Pushing for recent and specific examples is the key.
The lack of examples typically exposes the glaring omission. Rather than say, “I told you so,” good leaders use this as a teaching opportunity.
Examples reflect the power of understanding. Asking people to provide them is a lens into their true actions and beliefs. Can you give me an example of that?
